claims.text: Untreated W–Cu composites exhibit phase separation and interfacial void formation.
Applying a nanoscale Ni coating to W surfaces before composite fabrication will produce a Ni-rich interfacial layer during sintering.
A controlled thin Ni coating will stabilize the W–Cu interface.
The Ni treatment will suppress phase separation in the W–Cu composite.
The Ni treatment will suppress interfacial void formation in the W–Cu composite.
The Ni-enriched interfacial layer may contain transient or thin intermetallic phases.
The Ni-enriched interfacial layer reduces the interfacial energy between W and Cu.
Lowering interfacial energy enhances bonding at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni coating improves atomic-diffusion compatibility between the interfacial constituents.
Enhanced bonding and diffusion compatibility inhibit phase separation and void formation.
Improved interfacial stability maintains more continuous thermal pathways during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Reduced void density and phase separation will improve thermal conductivity.
The Ni-treated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an untreated composite under comparable processing and service conditions.
The intervention is expected to be effective when the Ni coating has a nanoscale thickness and processing permits controlled Ni diffusion.
The intervention may lose efficacy outside controlled Ni-diffusion regimes or at thermal fluxes and irradiation levels substantially above those tested.
